title: Guiding center quantization of a quantum Hall analog of Hawking radiation
authors: Rodrigo Andrade e Silva, Ted Jacobson
abstract: We revisit the quantum Hall analog of Hawking radiation in which a Fermi sea of electrons occupying half of a plane, subjected to a quadrupolar electric potential, gives rise to analog Hawking radiation of chiral edge modes. We show that the phenomenon is accurately captured by quantization of the classical guiding center theory, where the gyroscopic motion of the electrons is coarse grained and only the drift motion is resolved. The quantum dynamics takes place on a non-commutative plane, which requires an electron localized in the half-plane to be supported everywhere along the edge direction. This kinematical constraint on the quantum state leads directly to the radiation, which propagates in both directions away from the origin along the edge. The radiation is thermal with respect to laboratory time, which is equal (up to a constant factor) to the boost angle in the analog Minkowski spacetime in which the chiral edge modes propagate, so in fact it corresponds to analog Unruh radiation.
summary: This work analyzes the quantum Hall effect in a setup designed to mimic Hawking radiation. By quantizing the guiding center motion, the authors demonstrate that the chiral edge modes emit thermal radiation corresponding to the Unruh effect. This confirms that condensed matter systems can serve as powerful, controllable analogs for fundamental quantum gravity phenomena.
main_problem: The paper revisits the quantum Hall analog of Hawking radiation to show that the phenomenon can be accurately captured by quantizing the classical guiding center theory.
main_result: The quantization of the guiding center theory successfully reproduces the thermal spectrum characteristic of Hawking/Unruh radiation, confirming the analogy between chiral edge modes and curved spacetime horizons.
method: The analysis employs canonical quantization on the effective guiding-center action, utilizing techniques from quantum field theory in curved spacetime, including the Bogoliubov transformation approach for vacuum definition.
model_or_system: The system is a Fermi sea of electrons in a half-plane subjected to a quadrupolar electric potential and a uniform magnetic field, creating chiral edge modes analogous to those near a black hole horizon.
key_observables: The thermal spectrum of the emitted radiation, characterized by a temperature $T = \hbar\kappa / 2\pi$, and the non-zero, unequal probability current across the effective horizon.
important_parameters: The surface gravity $\kappa = \lambda/B$, the magnetic length $\ell = \sqrt{\hbar / qB}$, and the temperature $T$.
main_assumptions: The guiding center approximation is used, neglecting perpendicular kinetic energy; the analysis relies on the correspondence between lab time and the boost angle in the analog spacetime.
figures_summary: Not specified by notes, but the analysis involves solving time-dependent Schrödinger equations in $x$ and $y$ bases and deriving probability current conservation equations.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from setting up the physical model and the guiding center theory, deriving the effective edge spacetime metric, calculating the thermal spectrum via current conservation, and finally confirming the result by relating the in-vacuum and out-vacuum states using Bogoliubov transformations.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, condensed matter realization (Quantum Hall effect) for fundamental concepts in quantum gravity (Hawking/Unruh radiation), linking solid-state physics to general relativity in a solvable theoretical framework.
